newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS-Philips loosens Grundig ties further.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Philips loosens Grundig ties further.

text.p: Philips Electronics NV said on Wednesday it was further loosening ties with its Grundig unit, a move welcomed by analysts as reducing its exposure to the loss-making German consumer electronics firm.

Philips said it would act as a passive minority shareholder and from 1997 would account for Grundig's results only on a pro-rata basis related to its 32 percent stake, ending its previous 100 percent consolidation policy.

"We have given up our control over Grundig," said Philips spokesman Ben Geerts. "As a consequence we are deconsolidating Grundig, that means we only consolidate 32 percent of any losses during 1997," he said.
Shares in Europe's biggest consumer electronics firm rose 2.30 guilders, or 3.31 percent, to 71.70 guilders, outpacing a 0.82 percent rise in the AEX index of leading Dutch shares.

"It means that the results improvement at the consumer products division, at which Grundig used to be 100 percent consolidated, is going to have a significant boost for 1997," said Van Meer James Capel analyst Joost van Beek.
Philips said it was making the move as part of its policy to present a single brand in world markets and because of the negative returns from its investment in Grundig.
"From 1984 until December 31, 1995, Philips lost over 1.5 billion marks ($955 million) on Grundig," said Geerts.
Analysts said Wednesday's move was positive and showed the commitment of Philips chairman Cor Boonstra to deal with what he has called the company's loss-making bleeders.
"I guess it's another bit of evidence that things are happening sooner rather than later," said Schroders analyst Susan Anthony in London.
But Anthony said the market might be over-reacting somewhat to the news and, while Philips was attacking loss makers, it still had to show it could give consumers what they wanted.

"In a sense the cost-cutting part is the easier part...but to drive earnings growth in the future you really do need to see consumer electronics becoming a significant contributor," she added, which meant Philips had to turn its developments into commercial successes and get a return from them.
In February last year Philips said that from January 1, 1997 it would stop automatically reimbursing Grundig for its losses.
"The essence of what we announced last February was we gave up...the commitment to automatically reimburse Grundig's losses. We remained economically responsible for their losses," said Geerts.
The German company, famous for its televisions and hi-fi equipment, lost 250 million marks in 1996 and is seen by analysts as making a loss of about 135 million marks in 1997.

Geerts said Philips was in talks to unwind its contractual relationship with the Max Grundig Foundation, to which it pays a 50 million guilder ($28.5 million) a year dividend and which holds an option to sell Philips the 68 percent of Grundig it does not already own.

Since 1994 Philips has been making an 11 million guilder per quarter provision to buy out the Grundig stake by 2004, which analysts say could provide a war chest in any pay-off it might make to get out of the contract with the foundation.
Van Beek said he was raising his 1997 earnings estimate for Philips following the Grundig news to 6.75 guilders per share from his previous 6.50 guilders forecast.
Grundig on Wednesday said it would seek new partners and hold a news conference on Friday to give further details.

Asked about Philips's plans for its Grundig stake, spokesman Geerts said: "We are not planning to sell our Grundig stake, but one day someone could show up and ask us if we were willing to sell and then we would judge that at that moment." ($1=1.5711 Mark) ($1=1.754 Guilder)
